AT&T or Pfizer: Only One Gets My Dividend Dollars for the Next 10 Years ©Whitestudio2015 from Getty Images, Adam Simpson from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Pfizer yields 6.0% and AT&T yields 5.2%, and neither company raised its dividend in 2026.

AT&T's dividend took 44% of its free cash flow over the 12 months to Sept. 30, 2026, while Pfizer's took 89% over the 12 months to June 28.

AT&T expects free cash flow of $21 billion or more in 2028, while analysts expect Pfizer's revenue to shrink to $55.4 billion in fiscal 2028.

SpaceX's push into wireless is the main risk for AT&T, and patent losses on key drugs are the main risk for Pfizer.

Pfizer (PFE:NYSE) yields 6.0% and AT&T (T:NYSE) yields 5.2%. AT&T stock fell 8% on Oct. 23 after Bloomberg reported that SpaceX is in talks for access to at least 80,000 cell sites to build a competing wireless network.

Pfizer went the other way and raised its 2026 guidance on Nov. 3. So if I can only hold one of these dividends for the next 10 years, which one gets my money?

Source: TIKR and StockAnalysis, Nov. 9, 2026.

6 safe dividend stocks paying retirees 6%+ yields

There are over 100 stocks paying 6%+ annual dividends today.

But after an extensive investment review leveraging TIKR's proprietary data, we now believe only six of them are truly safe for retirees.

They're all yours for free as part of our new investment report, which you can access right here.

AT&T pays less, with plenty to spare

AT&T paid $1.11 a share in fiscal 2025, down from $2.08 in fiscal 2020, and its third-quarter release says it plans to keep the dividend at $1.11. What AT&T does have is cushion: over the 12 months to Sept. 30, 2026, its dividend took a well-covered 44% of free cash flow. Free cash flow has topped the dividends it paid in every fiscal year since 2016:

AT&T (T): free cash flow vs. dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2016–2025 (TIKR)

Management expects more: free cash flow of $18 billion or more in 2026, rising to $21 billion or more in 2028. Third-quarter revenue rose 5.3% from a year earlier to $32.3 billion. On the third-quarter call, CEO John Stankey made the case for fiber plus wireless: "the most durable customer combination in our industry is a fiber-fed broadband customer with a great wireless service on top of it, bar none."

Net debt is 3.3x EBITDA after AT&T's EchoStar spectrum purchase, and the company doesn't expect to get back to its 2.5x target until 2029. SpaceX also agreed on Oct. 8 to buy low-band spectrum from Grain Management for Starlink Mobile, a new threat to the wireless cash flow behind this dividend.

Pfizer pays more, with far less behind it

Pfizer's dividend is the bigger check, and its record is longer: the $0.43 a share it declared on Oct. 6 was its 352nd consecutive quarterly dividend. Pfizer paid $1.29 a share over the first nine months of 2026, so that fourth-quarter payment brings the year to $1.72, the same as fiscal 2025. Over the 12 months to June 28, 2026, the dividend took a risky 89% of free cash flow, and in two of the last three fiscal years, free cash flow fell short of it:

title: CalPERS Doubles $500 Million Bet Thanks to Elon Musk’s SpaceX Deal

CalPERS Doubles $500 Million Bet Thanks to Elon Musk’s SpaceX Deal
The black SpaceX logo is centered on a metallic silver background, representing the companys brand. (Credit: Photo: Norbert Maurice / Shutterstock - ejk )

California Public Employee's Retirement System has nearly doubled its investment in just over a year through a bet on radio spectrum that is now part of a major deal with SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX).

CalPERS, the largest public pension fund in the U.S., invested more than $500 million with Washington-based private equity firm Grain Capital, which acquired a portfolio of wireless spectrum licenses used to carry phone calls and text messages, sources familiar with the matter told Bloomberg.

SpaceX, which is working to expand its Starlink network into a director competitor to traditional wireless carriers such as AT&T (NYSE:T) and Verizon Communications (NYSE:VZ), agreed last month to purchase Grain's entire portfolio of 800-megahertz low-band spectrum licenses for $8 billion.

The acquisition gives SpaceX additional capacity to deliver cellular connectivity to devices indoors through its network of more than 10,000 satellites.

The transaction is expected to generate a distribution to paid in capital multiple of nearly two times for CalPERS, effectively returning at least $1 billion on its original investment, Bloomberg reported.

Read Also:Howard Marks Warns AI Investing Is a $1 Trillion Gamble: 'Practically Unknowable' Profits

CalPERS committed capital to Grain Specturm Holdings V in October 2025, a fund that subsequently acquired the 800MHz licenses from T-Mobile US Inc. (NASDAQ:TMUS), according to documents on the pension fund's website. CalPERS also invested in Grain's spectrum assets through a separately managed account.

The transaction, which still requires approval from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission, would enable SpaceX to integrate its satellite-to-cell technology with a ground-based network, expanding connectivity to devices across a broader range of locations.

The FCC has expressed support for developing next-generation satellite communications systems that can extend coverage to areas underserved by traditional networks while strengthening the U.S. position in the space-based telecommunications industry. The agency also established incentives encouraging spectrum owners such as Grain to partner with satellite operators like SpaceX.

Founded by David Grain in 2007, Grain Capital had initially targeted $6 billion from the sale of spectrum licenses before reaching the $8 billion agreement SpaceX.

Chicago, IL – November 11, 2026 – Zacks.com announces the list of stocks featured in the Analyst Blog. Every day the Zacks Equity Research analysts discuss the latest news and events impacting stocks and the financial markets. Stocks recently featured in the blog include: Space Exploration Technologies Corp. SPCX, AT&T Inc. T and Verizon Communications Inc. VZ.

Here are highlights from Tuesday's Analyst Blog:

Is SpaceX's $24B Texas Data Center Plan Worth Betting On?

Space Exploration Technologies Corp. is planning to develop a $24 billion gas-fired power plant and supercomputing facility at Starbase, TX, to expand its artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure and gain greater control over critical energy resources.

The company proposes to construct, own and operate the facilities on approximately 444 acres near Brownsville, TX, in a concerted effort to integrate energy generation, advanced computing and aerospace operations. By establishing a dedicated power supply alongside its computing infrastructure, SpaceX aims to accelerate capacity deployment, enhance cost predictability and strengthen its competitive position in the rapidly expanding AI market.

Strengthening AI Computing Capabilities

The proposed supercomputing facility could significantly expand SpaceX's AI infrastructure capabilities following its acquisition of xAI earlier in 2026. The investment would provide the company with an opportunity to develop additional computing capacity for training and deploying increasingly sophisticated AI models.

AI workloads require substantial computing resources and uninterrupted electricity supplies. Expanding in-house infrastructure could help SpaceX support growing demand for AI services while reducing its dependence on third-party computing providers. The investment could also enhance its ability to serve external customers seeking high-performance computing capacity, creating opportunities for incremental revenues over the long term.

Improving Energy Security and Operational Efficiency

The construction of an accompanying natural gas-fired power plant is another key advantage of the proposed development. By generating electricity on-site, SpaceX could reduce its reliance on external utilities and avoid lengthy delays associated with connecting large data centers to Texas' electricity grid.

Access to a dedicated electricity supply could enable the company to deploy computing infrastructure more rapidly and maintain greater control over operating conditions. This is particularly important for AI data centers, where reliable power availability is critical for maximizing computing utilization and minimizing operational disruptions. Owning its power generation infrastructure could also improve long-term energy cost visibility, potentially supporting operating margins as computing demand scales.

title: ASTS Q3 Earnings Call Highlights Service Rollout and Launch Plans
detail:
ASTS Q3 Earnings Call Highlights Service Rollout and Launch Plans
Zacks Equity Research
Wed, November 11, 2026 at 7:00 AM MST 4 min read
ASTS
T
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

AST SpaceMobile, Inc. ASTS centered its third-quarter 2026 earnings call on plans to activate intermittent satellite broadband service before year-end, expand launch capacity and accelerate satellite manufacturing.

Analysts pressed for clarity on deployment timing, commercialization and the economics of in-house launches.

ASTS Targets Initial Service Before Year-End

Founder, chairman and CEO Abel Avellan said the company remains on track to activate intermittent nationwide coverage in the United States and other key markets by the end of 2026.

Initial partners span the United States, Canada, Japan, Saudi Arabia and the United Kingdom. Avellan also highlighted a successful satellite-to-terrestrial network handover demonstration with AT&T.

During questions from William Blair, president and chief strategy officer Scott Wisniewski clarified that the first activation provides partners with coverage when satellites pass overhead. End-user beta trials are expected in early 2027, preferably with about 25 satellites operating.

AST SpaceMobile Sets a Faster Manufacturing Pace

Avellan said AST SpaceMobile expects to reach production of six ASIC-equipped BlueBird satellites per month in December. The company has manufacturing work underway through BlueBird 51.

The next-generation ASIC will enter production starting with BlueBird 34 rather than BlueBird 50, delivering a tenfold improvement in processing bandwidth relative to Block 1 spacecraft.

Management targets roughly 45 BlueBird satellites in orbit by mid-2027. During the Q&A, Avellan confirmed that BlueBird 11 deployed successfully despite taking longer to unfold, and said its deployment did not require a satellite redesign.

ASTS Expands Launch Options With Blacklift

Avellan described Blacklift as a reusable 20-ton rocket designed to carry as many as five BlueBird satellites into low Earth orbit per launch, beginning in late 2028.

The project draws on Firefly Aerospace engine technology. Wisniewski said ASTS expects several hundred million dollars of incremental capital expenditures in 2027 to advance the project.

Analysts from BofA Securities and Deutsche Bank questioned technical risks and the economics of internal launches. Management emphasized simplified rocket design and potential long-term cost reductions but did not provide a breakeven timetable.

AST SpaceMobile Adds Sovereign and Defense Funding

Wisniewski detailed approximately $1 billion of nondilutive Japanese funding for the J-LEO satellite program with Rakuten. Most funding proceeds are expected during 2027.
